lines.t: Hello! Welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
Hi! I'm Sam. Today we talk about neighbours.
I have a very good neighbour. His name is Mr Aliyev. He has a grey moustache and a checked shirt.
I met him on Saturday. I knocked on his door. I said, "Excuse me."
What did he say?
"Come in. Sit down. Tea."
[laugh] Always. He turned off the TV, right?
Yes! He turned off the TV and he made tea. I asked, "Can you help me with my phone?" He said, "First, tea."
How many cups did you drink?
Five. I said, "Thank you very much." Then he gave me another cup, one more cup. Every time!
That is the rule in our street. No noise from Mr Aliyev. But a very loud kettle.
Now my street is quiet, very calm. But my heart is loud. I can't sleep.
[laugh] That is Mr Aliyev's tea. Good night, Sam. Bye for now!

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is neighbours. And I have a small problem with mine.
Is it the noisy one?
Yes. Every night at eleven there is music in the flat upstairs. It's a very loud drum.
Did you talk to him?
Yes. I went up, and I said, "Hello! Nice to meet you. Could you turn it down, please?"
And?
He said, "Of course!" And he invited me in. It was a drum lesson. For forty children.
[laugh] At eleven o'clock?
Yes. His students are night owls. Now I borrow his earplugs, and he lends me his sugar. We are friends.
See? A good neighbour is a favour, not a problem. Mr Aliyev has the best garden in the street, and he says, "Let me know if you need anything."
And what do you need?
I need a lift to work. He always drives past my building.
Maybe I should move in with Mr Aliyev.
He would drop by every ten minutes with tea.
I know. That's why I'm staying. See you next time!

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is neighbours and community — and the oldest neighbour in Baku.
Mr Aliyev. Retired, bald, grey moustache, checked shirt. He restored his own samovar, and he gives figs to everyone.
Last week the lift in his building broke. He's eighty. He lives on the seventh floor.
The tenants called the landlord, who said, "I will fix it next month." That's a typical complaint.
So the community did something. Twelve neighbours worked out a timetable. Each person carries Mr Aliyev's bags on a different day.
That's what I call looking after each other. People don't always get along, but they lend a hand.
And he trusts everybody. He says thank you with tea and a plate of figs. He's very generous.
Not everyone is like that. Some neighbours gossip about everything. A fourth-floor lady knows my whole life, and I've never talked to her.
Well, I put up with a drummer upstairs. The key is to stay polite. And to live a stone's throw away from someone who bakes.
In England, do you know your neighbours?
In my street, everyone keeps themselves to themselves. Maybe too much. Here, I think I'd get fat.
A question for our listeners: do you know your neighbours' names? And what would you do for them?
Mine would carry the bags. See you next time!

words.en: the people who live in one area
no longer working because of age
find an answer or make a plan together
live quietly, not talking much to neighbours
